topic: Adaptive / difficulty-aware routing and compute allocation for LLM agent pipelines (applied to graph-eng)

findings.claim: RouteLLM: a router predicts, per query, the win probability of the strong model and sends the query to the strong model when it is >= a threshold alpha in [0,1]. With augmented training (Arena + GPT-4-judge labels), the best router (matrix factorization) reaches 95% of GPT-4 quality on MT-Bench with ~13.4% GPT-4 calls (random: ~49%). Cost savings vs always-strong: 3.66x on MT-Bench at CPT(50%), but only 1.41x on MMLU and 1.49x on GSM8K. Router overhead is <=0.4% of strong-model generation cost.
findings.evidence: Table values via WebFetch: MT-Bench CPT(50%) 13.40% (MF), 19.58% (BERT), 23.21% (SW), 31.50% (causal LLM); CPT(80%) 31.31%. GPT-4 ~$24.7/Mtok vs Mixtral ~$0.24/Mtok. Savings Table 6: 3.66x/2.49x MT-Bench, 1.41x/1.14x MMLU, 1.49x/1.27x GSM8K.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Savings are very task-distribution dependent (3.7x on easy chat, ~1.4x on reasoning-heavy). A single threshold-on-predicted-difficulty gate is cheap (<1% overhead), so a classifier gate in front of graph-eng is worthwhile, but expect modest savings on coding tasks that are non-trivial. Expose the threshold as a calibratable knob (e.g. cheap mode when P(simple) >= alpha).

findings.claim: RouteLLM routers trained only on generic preference data (no in-domain data) perform near random on MMLU and GSM8K (best CPT(50%) 45.0% and 53.6% vs ~50% random). Gains require in-domain labels: ~1,500 golden MMLU labels (<2% of training data) or GPT-4-judge labels. Overfit-prone high-capacity routers (BERT, causal LLM) are near random without augmentation. Evaluated only on public benchmarks and two-model routing.
findings.evidence: MMLU Arena-only best MF 45.00%; GSM8K Arena-only best MF 53.59%; after augmentation MMLU 35.4-41.3%, GSM8K causal LLM 33.64%. Authors list limitations: public benchmarks only, two-model only, dependence on in-domain/judge labels.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Do not rely on an off-the-shelf generic difficulty classifier for coding tasks. Use graph-eng's own run history (the benchmarks in docs/benchmarks) as labels, or use cheap rule-based/structural signals first. Start with a conservative rule gate and log features for later learned calibration.

findings.claim: FrugalGPT: LLM cascade (weak -> strong, stop when a learned scorer deems the answer good enough) can match the best single LLM (GPT-4) with up to 98% cost reduction, or improve accuracy by 4% at the same cost. The stop decision is a learned answer-quality scorer with a threshold per cascade stage; one third-party blog claims a DistilBERT-size scorer (unverified).
findings.evidence: Abstract-level numbers confirmed via WebSearch result snippet of arXiv abstract; PDF text was not extractable by WebFetch (compressed), so scorer details/per-dataset thresholds not verified. Blog claim about DistilBERT (https://mohakchugh.is-a.dev/blog/llm-routing-cascade-inference-cost-quality-optimization) unverified.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: graph-eng's natural cascade is: run cheap lean path first (single implement + verify), escalate to plan/design/review only if a gate fails. The 'scorer' can be execution-grounded (tests/verifier result) rather than a learned model, which is stronger for code. Headline 98% is an upper bound on easy QA datasets, not coding agents.

findings.claim: AutoMix: few-shot self-verification by the small model estimates answer correctness; a POMDP router handles noisy verification and chooses the model size; reports >50% compute cost reduction at comparable performance across 5 models and 5 datasets.
findings.evidence: Abstract only; no numeric thresholds or self-verification accuracy available in the fetched content.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Self-reported confidence from the cheap model (Haiku) is a noisy signal; treat it as one feature combined with external signals (test pass, diff size) and escalate on disagreement rather than trusting a single self-verdict. Supports 'verify -> escalate' loop design with a noisy-verifier assumption.

findings.claim: For coding agents, task-text-only routers are weak because a similar issue text can be a localized typo or a multi-module refactor. SWE-Router instead lets a cheap model run K=1-4 exploratory turns and routes on the partial trajectory (value head: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B + LoRA). On SWE-Bench Verified Route-AUC: text-only embedding routers 0.47-0.57 (near chance 0.5) vs trajectory routers 0.69-0.78 (e.g. deepseek-v3.2->gemini-3-pro: K=0 text 0.627, K=2 0.780, +15.3pp).
findings.evidence: Table 2 via WebFetch of HTML. Escalated runs pay the K weak turns and restart the strong model from scratch. No transfer on one split (SS-test with gpt-5-mini), AUROC did not track routing quality, Route-AUC unstable across repo distribution shift. No numeric matched-quality cost saving reported; threshold tuned on validation, value not published.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Best predictor of 'simple' is behavior after a short cheap probe, not the prompt. Implement a scout/probe step: run a cheap model (or Haiku) for 1-3 turns of repo exploration, then decide lean vs full flow from observed signals (files touched, number of modules, tests found). Budget the probe cost and design escalation to reuse the probe's context instead of restarting.

findings.claim: Scrouting/SuperScout: a 7B searcher explores the repo first and writes a structured handoff; a router then picks among four frontier fixers using the searcher's hidden states plus task text. On the Python subset of SWE-bench Pro it resolved 159/266 (~59.8%) vs best single model 158/266 (~59.4%) at roughly one-fifth the cost per solve; searcher cost <0.5 cent/task. Ablation: always using the cheapest fixer with the handoff ties the routed system, so the scouting handoff drives most of the gain, not the router; hidden states help cost routing but handoff text alone does not.
findings.evidence: WebFetch of the abstract page; calibration N=99 only, per-fixer effects described as directional. Full-text results not extractable.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Cheap upfront repo scouting + structured context handoff is the highest-value 'stage' to keep; it lifts cheap executors. Suggests graph-eng's planning could be replaced for simple tasks by a short scout that hands context to the Haiku executor, reducing the 624k-input-token executor blow-up by giving it targeted context.

findings.claim: Applied Compute trained a small router (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, GRPO, with read-only bash and 16K token budget) to choose among Nemotron 3 Ultra, Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5 per SWE-bench Verified task. Scores over 497 tasks: always-Opus 0.834, always-GPT-5.5 0.776, always-Nemotron 0.710, oracle 0.890, trained router ~0.76 (about GPT-5.5 quality at ~25% less cost). Nemotron ~$0.39/task; GPT-5.5/Opus roughly 3x. Signals kept: symbol referenced in >2 source files, rule consumed at >=2 stack layers (multi-file); signals dropped: stack traces, long problem statements, doc/build tasks. Rules accepted only if they beat the marginal best-model rate by >=15 percentage points (Wilson CI) and clear a cost-adjusted bar.
findings.evidence: Vendor blog (not peer reviewed). Binary reward with ties gave inflated misrouting (django-11211 example, router chose Opus, oracle Nemotron, both passed); partial credit (0.5 for ties) collapsed router onto Opus; authors prefer Total Variation Distance and Cohen's kappa vs oracle. No overall misroute rate reported. Oracle-router gap: 0.890 vs ~0.76 trained.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Concrete predictors of NOT-simple: multi-file / cross-layer changes (symbol used in >2 files). Long problem statements and stack traces were not predictive, so avoid prompt-length heuristics. Even a trained router leaves a large gap to oracle (0.76 vs 0.89), so build escalation, not just one-shot routing. Use >=15pp lift as a bar before adding a routing rule.

findings.claim: LiteLLM phase-based routing experiment: mini-SWE-agent on 12 SWE-bench Verified tasks, routing each tool call by phase (Explore -> deepseek-v4-flash, Verify -> haiku-4-5, Implement -> opus-5 high effort, opening -> sonnet-5; phase changes only after 2 consecutive calls). On the 9 tasks both solved: fixed Opus 9/9, $2.82 vs router 9/9, $1.51 (46% savings; $0.31 vs $0.17 per solved task), but 205 vs 112 LLM turns. Turn mix: explore 73% of turns but only $0.14 of cost; Implement 14% of turns, $2.56.
findings.evidence: Tiny sample (n=12, headline restricted to 9 mutually solved tasks; router resolve rate over all 12 not reported). Vendor blog.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Cost concentrates in the implementation/strong-model phase; exploration is cheap. Putting a strong model only where edits happen and cheap models on exploration/verification mirrors graph-eng's Haiku executor, but note that more turns can raise latency (graph-eng already 5-8x slower than single agent). Evidence this supports phase-level, not task-level, model assignment.

findings.claim: Coding-agent cost studies: effort control alone cut mean billed cost per run from $0.2753 to $0.0696 (-74.7%) and full stack to $0.0490 (-82.2%) with success 15/15 in every arm (Sonnet 5, DeepSeek Harness, n=15 per arm); under Claude Code the effort controller cut ~19% and full stack ~27%. Multiple-approach prompts raised reasoning tokens 2.4-7.4x with no credible success benefit (baseline 96.5% vs branching 95.2%). Redundant verification cost 1.48x/2.36x/18.25x median at severity levels 1/2/3+ with no success gradient. A bounded-efficiency 'stop early' prompt had no cost penalty on well-specified tasks but caused 3/5 hidden-test failures vs 0/5 on an ambiguous spec.
findings.evidence: Fetched first 100k of 157k chars; SWE-bench effort appendix not read. Another snippet reported xhigh vs low effort adds 12-16k thinking tokens and 23-30 turns, 2.4-4.5x billed cost on hard tasks (search snippet from https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.01347, not verified in fetched text).
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Extra ceremony (branching, redundant review, deep-thinking) often adds cost with no success gain on well-specified tasks, supporting skipping plan-review/design-review on simple tasks. But 'stop early' framing fails on ambiguous specs (3/5 hidden-test failures), a direct analogue of the Faturamento false-DONE risk: spec ambiguity must be a hard escalation signal.

findings.claim: Google/DeepMind/MIT 'Science of Scaling Agent Systems' (180 configs, 4 benchmarks, 3 LLM families): multi-agent coordination helps on decomposable/parallel tasks (Finance Agent centralized +80.9%) but hurts strictly sequential tasks: every multi-agent variant degraded -39% to -70% on PlanCraft (hybrid -39.0%, decentralized -41.4%, centralized -50.4%, independent -70.0%). Gains shrink as single-agent baseline rises, with a decision boundary near ~45% single-agent accuracy. Tool-heavy tasks (T=16) penalize multi-agent (efficiency-tools beta -0.330). Coordination overhead vs single agent: independent 58%, decentralized 263%, centralized 285%, hybrid 515%. Error amplification: independent 17.2x, decentralized 7.8x, hybrid 5.1x, centralized 4.4x. Predictive model picks best architecture for 87% of held-out configs (R2 0.513 CV).
findings.evidence: Numbers from WebFetch of the arXiv HTML (first 100k of ~158k chars). Authors caveat thresholds as indicative of the study setup, not universal. Centralized orchestrator with validation contained error amplification best (4.4x).
findings.implicationForGraphEng: A strong single-agent baseline (already 15/15 and 31/31) is exactly where extra agent stages stop paying off; when single-agent accuracy is high and the task is sequential/tool-heavy (code editing), default to the single/lean path. Keep a centralized validating critic (best error containment) for hard tasks rather than many independent stages. Measured graph-eng overhead (e.g. 20 calls vs 2) is the same order as the 263-515% overheads reported.

findings.claim: How routers are evaluated and how often they misroute: LLMRouterBench (400K+ instances, 21 datasets, 33 models, 10 routers) evaluates with AvgAcc, Gain@R (vs random), Gain@B (vs best single), Gap@O (vs oracle), PerfGain, CostSave, ParetoDist. Key results: several recent routers including commercial OpenRouter fail to beat the Best Single model (OpenRouter PerfGain -24.7%); binary routers (HybridLLM, FrugalGPT) struggle to cut cost while keeping best-single accuracy; a substantial gap to oracle remains driven by model-recall failures: on the 410 test queries (11.9%) where at most 3 models are correct, routers pick a correct model only 24.6% (Avengers) and 23.2% (EmbedLLM) of the time. No single overall misrouting rate is published. RouterBench (2403.12031) reports simple routing performs well in several areas and some routers struggle to generalize to complex tasks/new models.
findings.evidence: Fetched first 100k of 132k chars; per-router Gap@O values are in a figure not captured. RouterBench claim from search snippet only.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Always benchmark the adaptive mode against 'best single' (a single strong agent) and oracle, not against full graph-eng; if adaptive does not beat single-agent on cost-at-equal-quality, it is not worth shipping. Expect misroutes concentrated on rare hard cases (only 1-3 solvers) which map to graph-eng's hard tasks: those need cheap detection of failure after the fact (verification) rather than perfect upfront prediction.

findings.claim: Anthropic guidance: start with the simplest solution and add complexity only when needed (sometimes no agent at all); agentic systems trade latency and cost for performance and that trade must be justified; routing pattern sends simple/common queries to smaller models and hard ones to stronger models; single optimized LLM calls with retrieval/examples are often enough.
findings.evidence: Only secondary summaries were retrieved via WebSearch (e.g. https://medium.com/accredian/building-effective-ai-agents-a-guide-from-anthropic-e66b533ff091); the primary page was not fetched in full. No numeric thresholds.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Conceptual backing for a router-in-front design with a cheap default path; verify wording on the primary page before quoting in docs.

openQuestions: No published, validated threshold exists for 'coding task simple enough to skip planning/review'. The closest evidence is multi-file/cross-layer signal (symbol referenced in >2 files), partial-trajectory probing after K=1-4 cheap turns, and spec ambiguity. These thresholds must be calibrated on graph-eng's own benchmark runs.

FrugalGPT scorer architecture, per-dataset thresholds, and RouteLLM threshold values per benchmark were not extracted (PDF text not readable by WebFetch); read the saved PDFs or arxiv HTML versions if exact numbers are needed.
SWE-Router and Scrouting full-text numbers: no percentage cost saving at matched resolution reported for SWE-Router; Scrouting per-fixer effects based on N=99 calibration only.

Overall misrouting rate for coding routers is not published anywhere found; only oracle-gap proxies (0.76 vs 0.89 pass; 24% recall on rare-solver queries). Early-exit (token-level / layer-level) and confidence-gating literature (e.g. token-level cascade uncertainty) was not covered with primary sources in this pass.

Several cited 2026 arXiv papers (2607.00053, 2608.04804, 2608.01347, 2606.22902 Agent-as-a-Router, 2602.16873 AdaptOrch) are recent and were only partially read; Agent-as-a-Router and AdaptOrch were seen in search results but not fetched.

Skipping rules for plan-review/design-review specifically (versus model routing) have little direct empirical support; evidence is indirect (extra verification/branching adds cost without gain on well-specified tasks, but 'stop early' fails on ambiguous specs). n=1 graph-eng benchmarks cannot validate a gate; need a multi-task suite with hidden false-DONE tests.

topic: Subagent-driven development and multi-agent coding: when splitting helps vs hurts, token multipliers, parallel researcher/synthesizer patterns

findings.claim: Multi-agent systems use about 15x the tokens of chat and agents about 4x; token usage alone explained 80% of performance variance on BrowseComp (95% with tool calls and model choice). Their orchestrator-worker setup (Opus 4 lead, Sonnet 4 workers) beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on an internal research eval.
findings.evidence: Fetched page: '4x chat', '15x', '80% of variance', '90.2%'. Upgrading to Sonnet 4 gave a bigger gain than doubling the token budget on Sonnet 3.7.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: The 15x multiplier is the research-case upper bound. graph-eng (18-20 calls, about 1.0-1.4x single-agent cost on these benchmarks) pays ceremony cost with no quality gain on easy tasks. Model quality beats extra tokens or extra agents, so spend the budget on the strong model only where risk is high.

findings.claim: Anthropic says multi-agent fits breadth-first, parallelizable work that exceeds one context window. It fits poorly where agents need shared context or have many dependencies, and it names most coding tasks as such a case. The task's value must justify the token cost.
findings.evidence: Page states domains requiring shared context or many inter-agent dependencies are 'not a good fit', 'most coding tasks' included, and that real-time coordination is still weak.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Coding is the weak case for multi-agent. Keep the serial plan->implement->verify skeleton only when the task has real cross-file coupling or high false-DONE risk. Allow parallel fan-out only for independent read-only work such as scouting, review and critique.

findings.claim: Effort-scaling rules embedded in the lead prompt: simple fact-finding uses 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls; direct comparisons use 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each; complex research uses 10+ subagents. Early versions spawned 50 subagents for simple queries. Vague delegation briefs caused duplicated work; briefs need an objective, output format, tool guidance and task boundaries.
findings.evidence: Fetched page lists these tiers and the 50-subagent failure.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: This is the direct precedent for adaptive graph-eng: a complexity classifier with explicit tiers that set agent count and call budget (for example tier 0 = 1 call, tier 1 = implement+verify, tier 2 = full flow). Embed the tiers and a per-tier call and token budget in the planner prompt, and require a structured brief for each node.

findings.claim: Parallel execution (lead spawns 3-5 subagents, each using 3+ tools in parallel) cut research time by up to 90% on complex queries. Subagents write outputs to external storage and pass lightweight references back, avoiding information loss and token overhead. The lead saves its plan to memory before the context is truncated, and a separate CitationAgent post-processes the result.
findings.evidence: Page: 'cut research time by up to 90%', 'artifact systems... lightweight references', plan saved to memory, CitationAgent.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Parallel researchers plus a synthesizer maps to a notes-file pattern. Each researcher writes notes to a file with source URLs, returns only a path and a short summary, and the synthesizer reads the files. The same file-reference passing would curb graph-eng's 624k-input-token executor call, which looks like accumulated context passed inline.

findings.claim: Errors compound in stateful agents, so the system resumes from checkpoints instead of restarting. Evaluation advice: start with about 20 real queries, use a single-prompt LLM judge with 0.0-1.0 score plus pass/fail, and keep human testing. A tool-testing agent that rewrote tool descriptions cut task time by 40%.
findings.evidence: Fetched page text.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: n=1 benchmarks are too thin to tune on. Build a small suite of about 20 tasks (simple, medium, hard, false-DONE traps) and measure cost, latency and hidden-test pass rate per tier. Keep checkpoints and resume in the pipeline.

findings.claim: Cognition's two principles: share context (full agent traces, not just messages) and recognize that actions carry implicit decisions, so parallel subagents make conflicting assumptions. The Flappy Bird split produced mismatched Mario-style and non-Flappy pieces. Default recommendation: a single-threaded linear agent, plus a compression model for long tasks. The post calls multi-agent collaboration fragile in 2025 and has no quantitative benchmarks.
findings.evidence: Fetched page (dated 2025-06-12; cognition.ai redirects to cognition.com). The page says it reports no performance numbers.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Opinion piece, not data, but it matches the benchmark: a single Opus agent matched graph-eng quality at lower cost. For implementation, the plan and design decisions must travel verbatim to the executor, and parallel executors should be avoided unless their file scopes are disjoint. Where planning and review do run, pass compressed decisions, not just a task summary.

findings.claim: Claude Code docs: use a subagent to isolate high-volume output (test runs, logs, searches) and return only a summary. Use the main conversation for iterative, multi-phase work that shares context and for quick targeted changes, because a fresh subagent has to regather context. Subagents do not see the parent conversation and must be briefed in the delegation prompt.
findings.evidence: Fetched page sections 'When to use a subagent' and 'Context isolation' (docs.claude.com redirects here).
findings.implicationForGraphEng: A cold-started subagent per phase re-reads the repo, which is a likely source of graph-eng's extra input tokens and latency. Route small tasks to a single continuous agent. Use separate agents only for noisy verification (test output) and for independent review.

findings.claim: Claude Code subagent mechanics: a per-subagent model field (haiku, sonnet, opus, inherit) routes work to cheaper models; tools can be allowlisted or denied; independent subagents can run in parallel (default cap 20 concurrent); nesting is allowed up to 3 levels by default; each returning subagent adds its report to the main context; subagents can be resumed with history intact; foreground subagents block and background ones run concurrently.
findings.evidence: Fetched page. The final 9.9k characters of the page were not read.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Matches graph-eng's Haiku executor and verifier. Resuming a subagent instead of respawning it is an alternative to a fresh executor call on each retry. Cap report sizes so synthesis context stays small.

findings.claim: Anthropic's 'Building effective agents' says to start with the simplest solution and add complexity only when measured results show it helps. It defines routing (classify the input, send it to a specialized path or a cheaper model), parallelization (sectioning and voting), orchestrator-workers (for multi-file changes whose subtasks are unpredictable), and evaluator-optimizer (only when criteria are clear and refinement measurably helps). Coding agents benefit from test feedback.
findings.evidence: Fetched page text.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: The adaptive design is the routing pattern. The first node classifies complexity and risk and picks a path. Review and critic loops (evaluator-optimizer) run only when there is a clear criterion, such as hidden-test risk or a change touching shared contracts. Tests should be the primary verifier, with a model critic as an escalation.

findings.claim: Agentless (arXiv 2407.01489) replaces an autonomous agent with a fixed three-phase pipeline (localization, repair, patch validation). It reports 32.00% on SWE-bench Lite (96 fixes) at a cost of $0.70 (the abstract does not give the unit explicitly), and the authors argue that agent-based approaches are verbose and complex and that the simple pipeline matches or beats them on performance and cost.
findings.evidence: Abstract page only. The cost unit was not confirmed as per-issue.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: A fixed, narrow pipeline with a validation step can beat open-ended agent loops. For easy tasks graph-eng can run a lean path (implement + test validation) instead of many LLM-decided phases. Do not quote the cost as per-issue.

findings.claim: SWE-agent (arXiv 2405.15793) reports pass@1 of 12.5% on SWE-bench and 87.7% on HumanEvalFix, and says the design of the agent-computer interface affects agent behavior and performance.
findings.evidence: Abstract page only. The details of the interface design and any cost limits were not on the page.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: A single agent with a good tool interface is a strong baseline, so interface quality (clear tools, concise outputs) matters as much as the number of agents. The single-agent baselines in the benchmarks (1-2 calls) are credible. A good tool interface for the Haiku executor may reduce the 624k-token spike.

findings.claim: OpenHands (arXiv 2407.16741, ICLR 2025) is an MIT-licensed platform for building agents with sandboxed execution and multi-agent coordination, evaluated on 15 benchmarks including SWE-Bench and WebArena. The abstract gives no scores, cost or delegation details.
findings.evidence: Abstract only. CodeAct and the sub-agent delegation mechanism were not on the page.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Only supports the general claim that delegation exists in a mature framework. Read the full paper before using it as evidence for or against graph-eng's design.

findings.claim: MetaGPT (arXiv 2308.00352) encodes SOPs into prompt sequences with assembly-line role assignment (agents verify intermediate results to reduce cascading errors). ChatDev (arXiv 2307.07924) uses a chat chain and 'communicative dehallucination' across design, coding and testing. Neither abstract page gives benchmark numbers, cost or time.
findings.evidence: Abstract pages only; the abstracts state qualitative claims (MetaGPT more coherent than earlier chat-based systems).
findings.implicationForGraphEng: graph-eng's role pipeline resembles the SOP/assembly-line pattern. These papers are weak evidence for cost-efficiency because they report no cost, and role ceremony can be a fixed overhead on simple tasks. Fetch the full-paper cost tables before citing.

findings.claim: The MAST study (Cemri et al., NeurIPS 2025) catalogs 14 multi-agent failure modes in 3 categories (system design issues, inter-agent misalignment, task verification) from 200+ traces in the first version and 1,600+ annotated traces in the data release. It finds failures mostly stem from system design and coordination rather than model limits, and that multi-agent gains over single-agent systems on popular benchmarks are often small.
findings.evidence: Taken from web search result summaries; the paper itself was not fetched. The category labels differ between v2 and v3. The finding on small gains was reported through the summary.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Task verification is one of the three failure categories, which supports keeping an independent verifier (test-based) even on lean paths and making false-DONE detection the thing that escalates a task to the full flow. Verify the 'small gains' statement in the paper before relying on it.

openQuestions: What is the per-phase token and latency breakdown of the graph-eng runs? Which phase caused the 624k-input-token executor call (inlined repo or file context, retry accumulation, or no resume)?
The MAST claim about small multi-agent gains comes from a search summary; fetch the paper to confirm it and the failure-mode counts.

Which signals predict complexity and risk cheaply (files touched, presence of hidden or acceptance tests, ambiguity of spec, cross-module coupling)? No source prescribes this, so it needs an internal benchmark with about 20 tasks.
OpenHands, SWE-agent, MetaGPT and ChatDev were read from abstracts only; full-paper cost and delegation details are still missing.
Agentless cost unit ($0.70) is unconfirmed as per issue, and Anthropic's 15x figure is for web research, not coding, so it should not be applied directly to graph-eng.

topic: Graph/DAG orchestration of LLM agents: adaptive graph shape per task, and cutting latency of sequential review chains (research for graph-eng adaptive complexity)

findings.claim: Anthropic's own guidance: use the simplest solution that works and add multi-step agentic structure only when simpler solutions fall short. Agentic systems trade latency and cost for performance. Recommended primitives are Routing (classify input, send to a specialized path; easy queries to a smaller model like Haiku, hard ones to Sonnet), Parallelization (sectioning of independent subtasks; voting of the same task run several times, e.g. several code-review prompts), and Evaluator-optimizer (only when clear criteria exist and iteration adds measurable value).
findings.evidence: WebFetch of the page; the summary paraphrases routing, parallelization and evaluator-optimizer sections.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: This matches the benchmark gap: a single Opus agent (15/15 chess, 31/31 faturamento) at 1-2 calls was equal in quality and 3-8x faster. Add a cheap up-front router (complexity and risk classification) that picks a fast path. Parallel review by sectioning or voting should replace serial plan-review followed by design-review.

findings.claim: MaAS (Multi-agent Architecture Search via Agentic Supernet) optimizes a probabilistic distribution over agentic architectures and, for each query, samples a query-dependent system, so resource use matches the query's difficulty and domain. It reports using only 6% to 45% of the inference cost of existing handcrafted or automated multi-agent systems, with 0.54% to 11.82% better performance across six benchmarks.
findings.evidence: WebFetch of the arXiv abstract. The page did not give sampling mechanics, and I fetched it by arXiv id without a search hit, so the title and authors are not independently confirmed.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: This is the strongest published precedent for per-task adaptive graph shape. graph-eng can use a simplified version: instead of a learned supernet, a rule-based or LLM-scored selection among a few predefined skeletons (fast, standard, full) driven by task features.

findings.claim: AgentPrune does one-shot pruning of the spatial-temporal message-passing graph of a multi-agent system, removing redundant or unnecessary communication edges. It reports 28.1% to 72.8% fewer tokens, and comparable quality at $5.6 versus $43.7 for state-of-the-art topologies.
findings.evidence: WebFetch of the arXiv abstract. The arXiv id was supplied from memory, but the fetched page content matched the AgentPrune topic.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: This supports dynamic pruning. Start from the full template (plan, plan review, design, design review, implement, verify, critic, synth) and prune edges and nodes. Measuring which nodes rarely change the outcome, from the existing run logs, is the offline analogue of this.

findings.claim: G-Designer builds a task-aware communication topology with a variational graph auto-encoder, encoding agents plus a task-specific virtual node and decoding a topology adapted to the task. It reports token reductions of up to 95.33% on HumanEval. ARG-Designer and AgentConductor (an LLM orchestrator that builds a density-aware layered DAG per query, aimed at competition-level code generation) generate the graph from scratch per query instead of pruning a template.
findings.evidence: Search snippets only for these pages. I did not fetch the full papers. The 95.33% figure is a best-case HumanEval number.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Two designs are possible: prune a template (AgentPrune, G-Designer) or compose from scratch (ARG-Designer, AgentConductor). AgentConductor targets code tasks, so it is the closest analogue and worth a full read before designing the complexity classifier. For a deterministic Node.js engine, template pruning is cheaper and more auditable.

findings.claim: AFlow treats workflow design as search over code-represented workflows (LLM-invoking nodes plus edges) using a Monte Carlo Tree Search variant with LLM-driven expansion, execution feedback and experience backpropagation. It reports a 5.7% average gain over baselines across six benchmarks, and smaller models outperforming GPT-4o on specific tasks at 4.55% of its inference cost. The abstract does not say whether workflows are per task type or per query.
findings.evidence: Abstract only. The PDF fetch returned unreadable binary. A secondary summary quoted 19.5% over automated methods, which conflicts with 5.7% over SOTA, so treat either number with care.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: AFlow searches offline per benchmark or task family, not per query. For graph-eng this suggests a two-level approach: offline use the benchmark harness to find which skeleton works for which task class, then online pick by classifier. The strong claim that cheap executors can match big models fits the Haiku implement/verify design, but the 624k-token executor call shows the executor's context needs capping.

findings.claim: GPTSwarm models agents as computational graphs (nodes are operations such as LLM queries or tool use, edges carry information, graphs can be nested). It has node optimization (prompts) and edge optimization (connectivity), and reports gains on MMLU, Mini Crosswords, HumanEval and GAIA.
findings.evidence: Search summary of arXiv 2402.16823 (ICML 2024). Not fetched in full. Numbers such as 2.1% MMLU came from a review summary.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Edge optimization is the formal version of 'skip or add a review edge'. Graph-eng's edges (plan to review to design) can carry learned or configured keep/skip probabilities, tuned from the benchmark results.

findings.claim: Graph of Thoughts models LLM reasoning as an arbitrary graph (nodes are thoughts, edges are dependencies) with generate, aggregate (merge) and refine transformations. On sorting it reports 62% higher quality than Tree of Thoughts with over 31% lower cost.
findings.evidence: Search summary only (ETH Zurich, AAAI 2024). The result is for a synthetic task like sorting, not coding agents.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: The aggregate operation justifies merge nodes, for example combining plan and design into one call for small tasks, or merging verify and critic. Be careful extrapolating: the reported gain came from decomposition of a divisible task, not from review chains.

findings.claim: LangGraph execution is Pregel-style super-steps. A node with several outgoing edges, or a conditional edge returning a list, runs all targets in parallel in the next super-step. Send gives dynamic fan-out with per-branch state when the number of branches is only known at runtime. Parallel writes to the same state key need reducers. Command lets a node update state and route in one step. Recursion limit (1000 super-steps as of 1.0.6) bounds dynamic loops, and RemainingSteps lets a graph route to a fallback first.
findings.evidence: WebFetch of the official Graph API doc.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Concrete primitives to copy in the Node.js DAG scheduler: (1) a router function after plan that returns the next node set, including empty set to skip; (2) a parallel branch for reviewers with a deterministic reducer that merges findings; (3) a hard step and budget limit with a fallback path to synth.

findings.claim: Speculative Actions: a fast Speculator predicts the slow Actor's next action and pre-launches the downstream calls. If the guess matches, it skips ahead; otherwise it discards the work, so the final trajectory equals sequential execution (lossless). Results: about 19.5% time saved on chess with 3 predictions at 54.7% accuracy; 22-38% of API calls predicted correctly on tau-bench retail; about 20% end-to-end speedup headline; theoretical ceiling near 50%. Limits: only safe for reversible, idempotent or sandboxed side effects; extra token cost; mainly single-step.
findings.evidence: WebFetch of the paper's HTML version (arXiv 2510.04371).
findings.implicationForGraphEng: For graph-eng, the analogue is to start the next stage (design, or implement) speculatively while the plan review is still running, and discard it if the review returns a blocking finding. Implementation writes files, so it must run in an isolated worktree or scratch dir to be safe. Expected gain is modest (about 20%), and costs extra tokens on mismatch, so use it only on the full flow, not as the main fix.

findings.claim: Newer speculative-execution work for agents: Dynamic Speculative Planning tunes how many steps ahead to speculate, trading latency against cost (30% lower cost than the fastest lossless baseline); PASTE (Act While Thinking) speculates on tool execution from observed patterns and reports 48.5% lower average task completion time; Speculative Macro Commit reports 18.59% lower latency than sequential on tau2-Bench Telecom and 44.9% lower wall time on AppWorld; a search-agent speculation paper warns that extra requests can degrade serving speed under high concurrency.
findings.evidence: Search snippets only. I did not open these papers. Two of the arXiv ids (2609.03236, 2607.12236) are very recent relative to my knowledge, so check the pages exist and say what the snippet says before citing.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: The pattern is consistent across papers: speculation depth should be adaptive and capped, because wrong guesses waste compute. For graph-eng, cap speculation to one stage ahead and make it opt-in per complexity class.

findings.claim: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST) identifies 14 failure modes in 3 categories: specification issues, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification and termination. Interventions such as better role specification and orchestration gave +14% for ChatDev but did not fix everything.
findings.evidence: Search summary. Dataset size is reported inconsistently across secondary sources (200+ tasks over 7 frameworks vs 150 traces), so use only the arXiv or NeurIPS numbers.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Verification and termination is a major failure category, which is the false-DONE risk the faturamento benchmark targets. So the skip logic must not remove verification. Skip planning and design review on low-risk tasks, but keep an executable check (tests or acceptance) and a cheap final check.

openQuestions: Does AFlow produce one workflow per task family or per query? The abstract does not say. Read the full paper (PDF fetch returned binary; try arxiv.org/html or the ICLR page).

Which task features best predict when planning and review ceremony pays off (spec ambiguity, number of files or modules, presence of hidden acceptance tests, side-effect risk)? None of the fetched sources give a concrete classifier for coding tasks; AgentConductor (arXiv 2602.17100) is the most relevant to read in full.

No source found that directly measures parallel review versus sequential review chains for LLM code agents. The parallel-review recommendation rests on Anthropic's voting/sectioning guidance and LangGraph fan-out semantics, not a benchmark. This should be measured in the graph-eng benchmark.
Several speculation papers and two arXiv ids were seen only in search snippets and need verification before being cited in docs.
Why did one executor call reach 624k input tokens? No source here covers it; it is a context-management problem inside graph-eng, not a graph-shape one.
With n=1 per benchmark, the differences between graph-eng and the single-agent baseline cannot support claims about variance. More runs are needed before tuning thresholds.

topic: Economics of review/verification stages in LLM coding pipelines (plan/design review, critics, LLM-as-judge vs test verification, gating, multi-agent vs single-agent)

findings.claim: MAST taxonomy: 14 failure modes in 3 categories (system design ~44%, inter-agent misalignment ~32%, task verification ~24%), built from 1,600+ annotated traces across 7 MAS frameworks (taxonomy derived from 150 traces).
findings.evidence: Per-mode figures: step repetition 15.7%, reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%, unaware of termination 12.4%, disobey task spec 11.8%; verification: incorrect verification 9.1%, no/incomplete verification 8.2%, premature termination 6.2%. Category totals are summed from per-mode figures by the fetch summarizer.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Most multi-agent failures come from design and coordination (spec disobedience, step repetition, context loss), not lack of reviewers. Each extra stage adds hand-offs where these failures occur. The false-DONE risk (verification) is about a quarter of failures, so verification is worth keeping but should be grounded, not just more LLM reviewers.

findings.claim: A verifier is not a silver bullet: many verifiers do only superficial checks (e.g. does it compile). MetaGPT had about 1.56x more verification failures than ChatDev despite having a verifier. Adding a high-level task-objective verification step to ChatDev improved success by 15.6% on ProgramDev.
findings.evidence: Summarized from the paper's analysis section by WebFetch (only the first ~100k of 161k chars read). Same-model workflow/role-spec fixes gave about +9.4%; prompt-level fixes were described as inconsistent.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: What matters is verifier quality (checks against the task objective and hidden-test-like behaviour), not verifier count. Keep one strong objective-level verification and drop redundant review ceremony on simple tasks.

findings.claim: Google Research scaling study (180 configs, 3 LLM families, 4 benchmarks): once the single-agent baseline exceeds about 45% accuracy, adding agents gives diminishing or negative returns; the mean multi-agent change was about -3.5% with high variance; on sequential planning (PlanCraft) every multi-agent variant lost 39-70%; tool-heavy tasks suffer most from coordination overhead; independent agents amplify errors about 17.2x vs about 4.4x for centralized.
findings.evidence: Centralized coordination helped parallelizable finance reasoning (+80.8%). Predictive model picks best architecture for 87% of held-out configs (R^2 about 0.52 in v1; later version reports 260 configs/6 benchmarks and R^2 0.373, so figures vary by revision).
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Strong support for adaptive gating: a capable single agent already near saturation on simple tasks should not get extra agents. Use a cheap complexity or capability signal (task size, tool count, parallelizability) to choose topology. A central orchestrator beats independent agents for error containment.

findings.claim: Anthropic's guidance: find the simplest solution and add complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes. Evaluator-optimizer fits only when clear evaluation criteria exist and iterative refinement measurably helps. Coding agents should get ground truth from the environment (test results, code execution) at each step.
findings.evidence: Direct fetch of the primary source. It also notes that human review is still needed for broader system fit and that a single optimized LLM call is often enough.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Supports tiered flow: single-pass for simple tasks, with test execution as the main feedback loop. LLM critic loops only where criteria are clear and an improvement is measurable.

findings.claim: Anthropic multi-agent research system: agents use about 4x chat tokens and multi-agent systems about 15x. Multi-agent suits high-value, heavily parallelizable work. It is a poor fit for tasks needing shared context or many inter-agent dependencies, and coding is called out as having fewer parallelizable subtasks. Effort-scaling rules embedded in prompts: simple fact-finding gets 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls.
findings.evidence: Direct fetch of the primary source.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Gives a precedent for explicit effort-scaling rules (agent and call counts by complexity). The 15x multiplier is consistent with graph-eng's 18-20 calls vs 1-2 for a single agent. Graph-eng's coding work is mostly sequential and coupled, the case where multi-agent pays least.

findings.claim: Cognition argues parallel multi-agent systems are fragile because sub-agents lack each other's context and make conflicting implicit decisions. It recommends a single-threaded linear agent by default, narrow read-only sub-agents, and consolidating decisions. Edit-apply pipelines splitting planning and editing across models were error-prone.
findings.evidence: Practitioner blog post (2025), not a controlled benchmark.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: A plan -> design -> Haiku implement hand-off loses context. One executor call hit 624k input tokens, which suggests context is being re-shipped. Pass full traces or artifacts to the implementer, and skip the split on tasks small enough for one agent.

findings.claim: Agentless: a fixed three-phase pipeline (localization, repair, patch validation) with no agent autonomy reached 32.00% on SWE-bench Lite at $0.70 per issue, the best among open-source agents at the time. The authors found some benchmark issues had flawed ground-truth patches or misleading descriptions and built SWE-bench Lite-S.
findings.evidence: The abstract fetch did not detail how test-based validation or reranking works. v1 reported 27.33% at $0.34, and v2 added patch validation, which raised the solve rate and the cost.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: A lean fixed pipeline with test-based validation is competitive with heavy agentic scaffolds at a fraction of the cost. Test-based validation is the stage worth keeping.

findings.claim: Intrinsic self-correction (no external feedback) does not reliably improve reasoning and can degrade performance by flipping correct answers to wrong. Prior reported gains often relied on oracle labels or weak initial prompts.
findings.evidence: Huang et al. 2023 (ICLR 2024). Only the abstract and search summaries were seen. The abstract covers reasoning tasks, not coding pipelines specifically.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: A same-model LLM critic or plan reviewer with no new information is likely wasted or harmful. Reviews need an external signal (tests, execution, spec checks) or a different information source to pay off.

findings.claim: LLM-as-judge is useful but biased: GPT-4 judges agreed with humans more than 80% of the time on MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena, but showed position bias (GPT-4 consistent under swapped order only 65.0% of the time, Claude-v1 23.8%), verbosity bias (a repetitive-list attack fooled GPT-3.5 and Claude-v1 91.3% of the time vs 8.7% for GPT-4), self-enhancement bias, and weak reasoning on math.
findings.evidence: Figures come from search summaries of Zheng et al. 2023 Tables 2-3. Self-enhancement magnitudes were not confirmed. The results are for chat quality, not code correctness, and for older models.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Do not use LLM judges to gate correctness where tests can. Reserve them for fuzzy criteria (design fit, spec coverage), preferably from a different model, with explicit rubrics and shorter outputs.

findings.claim: Repeated sampling gains depend on verifier reliability: coverage grows roughly log-linearly with sample count (SWE-bench Lite solve rate for one open-source setup went from 15.9% to 56%), but gains are realized only if a checker such as unit tests can pick the right candidate. Weak or homogeneous test suites overstate quality, and LLM-generated verifier checks can look stronger than they are.
findings.source: https://scalingintelligence.stanford.edu/blogs/monkeys ; secondary preprints seen via search (not directly verified)
findings.evidence: Only a search snippet was seen. The claim about weak test suites comes from a separate paper that was not identified or fetched.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Self-consistency or best-of-n is only worth its cost with an automatic verifier. For the Faturamento tasks with hidden acceptance tests, investing in a stronger verification step (adversarial tests derived from the spec) beats adding more plan or design reviewers.

findings.claim: Cascades and routing: FrugalGPT reports matching GPT-4 with up to 98% cost reduction (best case) by querying cheap models first and escalating only when a reliability check fails, and beating GPT-4 accuracy by 4% at equal cost.
findings.evidence: The 98% figure is the paper's best case on its benchmarks. It requires labeled data and a trained scorer.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: This is the conceptual basis for risk-based gating: run the cheap path first and escalate to plan review, design review and critic only on a trigger (verification failure, large blast radius, ambiguity, low scorer confidence). Gating signals need cheap computation, for example test failures or task-size heuristics.

openQuestions: No direct controlled study was found that measures the marginal gain of a plan-review or design-review stage in LLM coding pipelines. The evidence here is indirect (MAST, scaling paper, self-correction), so graph-eng should measure this itself with ablations.

No source was found that evaluates risk-based gating thresholds specifically for coding (what features predict need for review). The Google scaling paper's predictive model and FrugalGPT cascades are the closest analogues.
The MAST fetch covered only the first 100k of 161k characters, so some intervention details may be missing.
The 624k-token executor call is not explained by any source. Check graph-eng's own context-passing instead.
The benchmarks are n=1 each, so the cost/latency gap is suggestive only. Repeat runs with variance are needed before generalizing.

No source was found for the claim that the stronger the single-agent baseline, the less review helps, applied to coding specifically. The 45% saturation threshold comes from non-coding benchmarks (finance, browsing, planning).

topic: OpenRouter Jev / Laya existence, pricing, API usage, and cheap classifier alternatives

findings.claim: Jev EXISTS on OpenRouter, published by TypeSafe. It is TypeSafe's first 'System One' model: a structured decision model, not a chat LLM. It takes a state plus typed questions and returns typed answers with probabilities. No text, reasoning or explanations.
findings.evidence: OpenRouter community guide: 'Jev is not an LLM. It returns typed answers with probabilities.' TypeSafe docs: 'Jev is TypeSafe's flagship model and the first System One model... doesn't write replies, produce code, or explain its reasoning.' This matches the user's 'System One' / 'TypeSafe' / Sept 2026 description.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Jev can only classify. It cannot plan, review or code. It could serve as a cheap task-complexity gate (choice: simple/moderate/complex, or noul/score for risk) ahead of the graph. It cannot replace any Claude agent in the flow.

findings.claim: OpenRouter model ids found for TypeSafe: typesafe/jev-1.13, typesafe/jev-1.14, typesafe/jev-router, and the alias ~typesafe/jev-latest. Do not use any other id.
findings.evidence: The author page lists exactly those four. The community guide says model is 'typesafe/jev-1.14' or '~typesafe/jev-latest', and that typesafe/jev-1.13 remains available. Jev Router is described as picking the best model and reasoning effort per request, running on Jev itself.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: If integrating, pin typesafe/jev-1.13 or 1.14 rather than the alias. Probabilities differ between versions, and TypeSafe says thresholds must be retuned per model.

findings.claim: Pricing: Jev 1.13 is US$0.042 per 1M input tokens (= $0.000000042/token) and US$0 per 1M output tokens. TypeSafe docs give the same price for 1.14. I could not extract a separate OpenRouter price for 1.14, because its page returned 404 or empty.
findings.evidence: OpenRouter providers page: '$0.042 input / $0 output per 1M tokens'. TypeSafe models page: both versions '$42 per Btok ($0.042 per Mtok)', input billed, output free. Responses include usage.cost in USD.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: A classification call with about 2k tokens of task text costs roughly US$0.00008. That is negligible next to the US$0.68-0.73 runs, so cost is not a constraint on adding a Jev gate.

findings.claim: Context length: OpenRouter lists 262K (262,144) tokens. TypeSafe's own docs say the default limit is 64k tokens per request and 32k per question. 262k needs the header TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true, which is slower and less accurate. The OpenRouter guide says text over about 32,000 bytes also falls into slower long-context mode.
findings.evidence: The sources disagree on the 'headline' context, but are consistent once the long-context mode is taken into account.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: For gating, send only the task description plus a short repo summary, kept well under 32KB. Do not send whole files.

findings.claim: Latency/throughput: no first-party latency or throughput figures were found. The OpenRouter model and providers pages list none, the TypeSafe docs and jaggedness page give none, and the OpenRouter guide says 'no latency figures'. The only number is a competitor-adjacent claim that Jev takes 236-276 ms per question, from the article announcing Laya.
findings.evidence: The article says Jev latency is 236-276 ms per question versus 32.8 ms p50 for Laya on a T4 GPU. The author is Laya's creator, so this is not independent.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Expect a sub-second gate. This still needs measuring in our environment before relying on it. Network round trip to OpenRouter adds to it.

findings.claim: Structured-output support: Jev does NOT use the OpenAI-style response_format/json_schema. It has its own typed primitives: choice (options with per-option probabilities and confidence), noul (probability of yes), score (ordered levels, up to 10, with probability-weighted score and confidence) and box (images, 1.14 only). Requests give state and a keyed questions object, and the output is already typed JSON by construction.
findings.evidence: Request: {model, state, questions:{name:{type:'choice'|'noul'|'score', instructions, criteria}}}. Choice criteria is an object of 1-255 entries. Score criteria is an array of 1-10. Responses: answers[name] = {type:'choice', choice, confidence, probabilities} etc., plus usage{input_tokens, output_tokens}. The OpenRouter guide also lists typesafe/jev-router as callable via the standard /api/v1/chat/completions, but I found no schema for what it returns.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: For complexity routing, ask a choice (trivial|simple|moderate|hard) plus noul questions such as 'touches money/billing', 'needs hidden-test-level edge cases', 'multi-module'. Combine them in deterministic code, with confidence gating that escalates to the full flow when uncertain.

findings.claim: Jev on OpenRouter has two endpoints: POST https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (the Decisions API) and POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (SDK-compatible). Auth is the OpenRouter key. TypeSafe's own direct endpoint is POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>. The model id there is jev-1.13.0, jev-1.14.0, jev-latest (=1.13.0) or jev-preview (=1.14.0).
findings.evidence: The OpenRouter guide says an OpenRouter API key authenticates both APIs and that no TypeSafe account is needed. The 'alpha' path suggests the endpoint may change. The docs do not show a full OpenRouter-specific request example for choice/noul/score, only for box, so the field names for those are inferred from TypeSafe's direct API.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Verify the request shape with one real call before building. Isolate it behind a small adapter so an alpha-endpoint change does not break the engine.

findings.claim: Benchmarks: no first-party benchmarks from TypeSafe. The only numbers are third-party, in Laya's announcement and measured by Laya's authors. Jev scored 0.727 on typed-decisions, 0.910 on AG News, 0.480 on DAIR Emotion and 0.870 on Banking77. Calibration error was 0.246. Jev beat Laya only on Banking77 (Laya 0.425).
findings.evidence: The article says the comparison is 'directional rather than controlled'. TypeSafe's models page gives no accuracy or latency figures and only links a jaggedness page.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Do not trust published accuracy for our domain. Build a small labelled set from our own tasks (chess, faturamento, plus easy/hard examples) and measure routing accuracy, especially the false-simple rate, before enabling any skip of review stages.

findings.claim: Known weaknesses of Jev 1.13 that matter for a complexity classifier: it reads instructions literally; it leans toward the first listed choice option; accuracy drops as irrelevant state grows; it is weak at counting, math, numeric and date comparison; and text meant to steer it can shift answers.
findings.evidence: Quoted directly from the jaggedness page. It gives no latency or benchmark figures.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Randomise or reorder choice options and check consistency. Keep the state short. Treat the task text as untrusted, because a prompt-injected task could try to downgrade itself to 'simple'. Keep hard rails in code, for example forcing the full flow when the task mentions money, billing, migrations, auth or acceptance tests.

findings.claim: Laya does NOT appear to exist on OpenRouter. No OpenRouter model page or id was found. The OpenRouter author listing for TypeSafe, the Jev guide's list of other decision models, and the pricing aggregator contained no Laya. Laya exists elsewhere: an open-weight (Apache 2.0) English decision model by Convai Innovations (Nandakishor Mukkunnoth), announced about 20 Sep 2026, self-hosted via pip install laya, with weights at huggingface.co/app2610/laya.
findings.evidence: Search surfaced only openrouter.ai/apps/url/...layla-network.ai, a different product called Layla. The Laya article says nothing about OpenRouter and says it is free self-hosted. Reported figures: about 33 ms per question on a T4 GPU (32.8 ms p50), 193-464 ms on CPU, calibration error 0.081. These are self-reported. I could not directly list the live OpenRouter catalog, so absence is based on the listings above, not a full catalog query.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Laya cannot be called through OpenRouter. Using it means self-hosting a Python model (about 33 ms per question on a GPU, 193-464 ms on CPU), which is a poor fit for a dependency-free Node engine. Treat it as not available for this purpose.

findings.claim: Other 'decision' models are listed in the OpenRouter Jev guide as using the same Decisions API (change only the model field): openai/gpt-6-luna-decisions, microsoft/microsoft-decision-1, perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2, perplexity/pplx-decider-flash-v1.2, cloudflare/clef, cloudflare/clef-flash, cloudflare/clef-omni, inception/mercury-decide, liquid/d1, liquid/d1-ultra, upstage/solar-decide, upstage/solar-decide-flash.
findings.evidence: The ids come from a fetch summary of the guide page. Direct OpenRouter model pages for openai/gpt-6-luna-decisions and cloudflare/clef-flash returned 404, so I could not confirm pricing or that these ids resolve. Do not use them without checking.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: If a decision-model gate is adopted, a vendor-neutral adapter lets us swap models. Probabilities are not comparable between models, so thresholds need retuning.

findings.claim: I could not find a verified price or latency for any decision model other than Jev. Closest cheap, fast, general models on OpenRouter that suit classification, with per-1M-token input/output prices from one aggregator dated Oct 2026: mistralai/mistral-nemo $0.029/$0.03 (131K); google/gemma-3-4b-it $0.04/$0.05 (131K); inclusionai/ling-3.0-flash $0.021/$0.063 (262K); meta-llama/llama-3.1-8b-instruct $0.05/$0.08 (131K); openai/gpt-oss-20b $0.018/$0.09 (131K); openai/gpt-5-nano $0.05/$0.40 (400K); openai/gpt-4.1-nano $0.10/$0.40 (1.05M); google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite $0.10/$0.40 (1.05M); anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 $0.10/$0.50 (1M); google/gemini-3.1-flash-lite $0.25/$1.50 (1.05M); google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite $0.30/$2.50 (1.05M).
findings.evidence: Prices are from a single third-party aggregator and cross-check imperfectly: another search snippet gave different figures for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ($0.014 vs $0.15/$0.60), so re-verify on the live OpenRouter model page before use. Latency was reported for only DeepSeek V4 Flash (median 0.76 s, p95 2.59 s, one workload on 2026-09-01) and GLM-5.2 (median 1.20 s, p95 3.69 s). Structured-output support is per provider endpoint, and I did not verify it per model above.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: A cheap general LLM with response_format json_schema is the fallback gate. At about 1-2k input tokens and about 100 output tokens, the cost is well under US$0.001 per task. No benchmark data exists for routing accuracy on our task types.

findings.claim: OpenRouter chat completions API for Node with no dependencies: POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions with headers Authorization: Bearer <OPENROUTER_API_KEY> and Content-Type: application/json. Optional app headers are HTTP-Referer and X-OpenRouter-Title. Body: model, messages [{role: system|developer|user|assistant|tool, content}], optional stream (default false), temperature, max_completion_tokens (max_tokens is deprecated, and some providers enforce a minimum of 16), response_format, provider, plugins, reasoning/reasoning_effort. Node's built-in fetch is enough.
findings.evidence: The auth page gives a fetch example using process.env.OPENROUTER_API_KEY and reading data.choices[0].message. The non-streaming response has id, object 'chat.completion', created, model, choices[{index, message{role, content}, finish_reason}], and usage{prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, total_tokens, cost, ...}. Streaming is SSE with chunk.choices[].delta and a [DONE] sentinel. The reference page was only read for its first 100K of 214K characters.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: A single fetch call with AbortSignal.timeout(...) is enough for a gate. Read usage.cost from the response for per-call cost accounting that matches what the benchmark reports.

findings.claim: JSON / structured output via the chat API: response_format supports type text, json_object, json_schema (object with name, strict, schema), grammar and python. Support is per provider endpoint, not per model. To force routing only to endpoints that support it, set provider: {require_parameters: true}. Unsupported models error. Invalid schemas error. With strict: true, schemas need additionalProperties: false and all properties required. A Response Healing plugin can repair invalid JSON on non-streaming calls.
findings.evidence: The structured-outputs guide gives this exact shape and says enforcement varies by provider: some guarantee conformance, others treat it as a strong hint.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Still validate the returned JSON in code and fall back to the full flow on any parse or schema failure. That makes the gate fail safe.

findings.claim: Timeouts and errors: OpenRouter documents no request-timeout parameter. The client must set its own (for example AbortSignal.timeout). Error body is {error:{code, message, metadata?}}. Codes: 400 bad params, 401 bad key, 402 insufficient credits, 403 permissions/moderation/budget, 408 request timed out, 429 rate limited, 502 model down or invalid response, 503 no provider meets routing needs. 524 appears in the API reference as an edge timeout. Errors during generation can arrive with HTTP 200 in the body or as an SSE event, so check for an error field even on 200. Retry 429, 503 and in-flight 402 with backoff using Retry-After (seconds); do not blindly retry 402 without it. Mid-stream failover stops once tokens have started.
findings.evidence: The errors page includes a fetch retry snippet that reads the Retry-After header. Typed provider timeouts map to HTTP 504 per the errors page.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: The gate must have a short timeout (for example 5-10 s), at most one retry, and a deterministic fallback to the full flow, so that a gate outage never lowers quality. TypeSafe's direct API adds 429 and 529 (overloaded) and a 32 MiB body cap.

findings.claim: Release date check: Jev 1.13 was released Sep 17-18, 2026 per OpenRouter (pages disagree by a day), consistent with the user's 'September 2026'. Jev 1.14 is available from October 14, 2026 per TypeSafe's docs.
