topic: Fast-path vs plan-then-execute in production agent tools; effort levels and thinking budgets; model selection; cost/latency vs quality of skipping planning

findings.claim: Claude Code's own best-practices doc says plan mode adds overhead and should be skipped for small, clear-scope tasks. Planning pays off when the approach is uncertain, the change touches multiple files, or the code is unfamiliar. Heuristic given: if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan.
findings.evidence: Doc states plan mode 'is useful, but also adds overhead'; typo/log-line/rename tasks should be done directly; planning most useful when uncertain about the approach, multi-file, or unfamiliar code.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Use this as the router rule. Fast path when the task fits a one-sentence diff, touches 1-2 files, has a known approach and is already verifiable. Full flow when it is multi-file, unfamiliar or ambiguous. The signals are cheap to compute from the scout context (files touched, spec ambiguity, checks available) before planning starts.

findings.claim: The same doc puts verification ahead of planning. Giving the agent a runnable check (tests, build, script diffing output) closes the loop. It also recommends an independent fresh-context reviewer subagent before treating work as done, and warns that a reviewer asked to find gaps will always report some, which leads to over-engineering unless it is told to flag only correctness or requirement gaps.
findings.evidence: Sections 'Give Claude a way to verify its work' and 'Add an adversarial review step'; warns that chasing every finding yields extra abstraction layers and defensive code.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: On the fast path replace plan, plan review, design and design review with one executable check (hidden-test style acceptance or the repo's tests) plus one independent critic, tuned to report only correctness or requirement gaps. That matches the Faturamento false-DONE concern at much lower cost. Add a severity filter to the critic prompt so it does not inflate work.

findings.claim: Claude Code's model config maps tasks to models and effort. haiku is for simple fast tasks, sonnet for everyday coding, opus for complex reasoning. opusplan uses Opus in plan mode and Sonnet for execution. Effort is low/medium/high/xhigh/max, with low for small edits or renames and medium for day-to-day work with clear scope. high is for bug fixes where verification and edge cases matter. max can overthink. The doc advises pairing model with effort, e.g. a capable model at medium for routine work.
findings.evidence: Tables 'Model aliases', 'Choosing a level' and 'Choosing a model' on the page; defaults are medium on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, high on most others.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Expose complexity tiers as (phase set, model, effort) triples, not just a phase set. Plan and critic roles get a strong model at medium or high effort, executors get Haiku or Sonnet at low or medium. opusplan is existing evidence that strong-plan with cheap-execute is the product's own default split, which validates graph-eng's Haiku executor.

findings.claim: Anthropic API docs: effort is the recommended control for thinking depth. It is a behavioral signal, not a strict token budget, and it applies to all output tokens, including tool calls and text. Low effort means fewer and terser tool calls and can skip thinking for simple problems. Claude Sonnet 5.5 guidance: for agentic coding, start with medium for well-specified tasks and move to high for harder or longer ones. Haiku 5.5 at low is more likely to skip a search, stop early or skip a check in long agent prompts.
findings.evidence: Sections 'How effort works', 'Effort with tool use', and per-model recommendations for Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5. Doc says 'Use low for speed-sensitive or simple tasks' and 'Consider dynamic effort: adjust effort based on task complexity'.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Pass --effort per node instead of using one global level. Caveat for the Haiku executor and verifier: low effort risks skipped checks, which is the false-DONE failure mode. Keep Haiku at medium for verify, or keep a deterministic check outside the model (run the tests, parse the exit code). Effort is a soft signal, so also bound cost with max-turns or a token cap per node.

findings.claim: Anthropic says thinking is adaptive: the model decides per request whether and how much to think, effort is the primary lever, and lowering effort is the recommended first lever before prompt-based steering. Prompt steering is wording-sensitive and may cut quality on tasks that need reasoning. On Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, asking in the prompt to think less does not reliably reduce thinking. Changing the top-level effort between requests invalidates the prompt cache, so vary effort across workloads, not within a cached conversation. Per-message effort (beta) preserves the cache. In an agent harness, the doc suggests nudging thinking up on planning steps and down on routine confirmations.
findings.evidence: Sections 'How Claude determines when to think', 'Steering how often Claude thinks' (warning box), 'Prompt caching' and 'Cost control'. There is no thinking-token budget on adaptive models; max_tokens is the hard cap.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Decide effort per node when the node is spawned (each graph-eng agent is a fresh CLI session, so the cache invalidation concern is smaller), not by prompt phrases. Treat 'think budget by difficulty' as an effort-tier table in config. Verify the tier on your own evals as Anthropic recommends: run the n=1 benchmarks again as a sweep.

findings.claim: Opus 4.5 launch claims: at medium effort it matches Sonnet 4.5's best SWE-bench Verified score with 76% fewer output tokens. At the highest effort it beats Sonnet 4.5 by 4.3 points with 48% fewer tokens. Anthropic positions effort as a way to minimize time and spend or maximize capability.
findings.evidence: Page text: 'With our new effort parameter on the Claude API, you can decide to minimize time and spend or maximize capability'; the 76% and 48% figures are on the page.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: A single strong agent at medium effort is a cheap baseline and is the obvious fast path (your single-Opus runs cost US$0.51-0.70 and took 105-180s). Number comes from Anthropic's SWE-bench Verified on an older model generation, so treat it as directional, not as a measured saving for graph-eng.

findings.claim: Anthropic's 'Building effective agents' says to find the simplest solution possible and add complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes. Agentic systems trade latency and cost for task performance. It describes a routing pattern that sends easy queries to smaller, cheaper models and hard ones to more capable models, and an orchestrator-workers pattern for multi-file code changes where subtasks are not known in advance.
findings.evidence: Key sentence: 'find the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed'; complexity 'only when it demonstrably improves outcomes'.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Frames the design goal: a cheap classifier or router in front of the pipeline, and a measurable gate for adding each ceremony phase. Each of plan review and design review should have to earn its call with evidence (a hard-task benchmark where it changes the result). On n=1 chess and Faturamento runs both reached full score with a single agent, so those phases did not show a quality gain.

findings.claim: Anthropic's multi-agent research system post: agents use about 4x more tokens than chat and multi-agent about 15x. Token usage alone explained 80% of the variance in BrowseComp performance (tool calls and model choice add most of the rest, 95% together). It embeds explicit effort-scaling rules in prompts: simple fact-finding gets 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons get 2-4 subagents, complex research 10 or more. It also says coding has fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research, so multi-agent suits it less.
findings.evidence: Direct quotes retrieved: 'multi-agent systems use about 15x more tokens than chats', 'Simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls', coding 'fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research'. Early versions reportedly spawned too many subagents for simple queries (secondary summaries; not confirmed in the fetch).
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Direct precedent for graph-eng's problem: Anthropic had to hard-code effort-scaling rules because the orchestrator over-spent on simple tasks. Put the same rule in the planner or router (explicit tiers with call-count ceilings). Also note multi-agent value is tied to task value, so expect the full flow to pay off only on genuinely hard or high-risk tasks. Coding's low parallelism supports the weaker case for ceremony on simple coding tasks.

findings.claim: Cursor, VS Code Copilot and Claude Code converge on the same rule: plan mode is opt-in, for uncertain or multi-part work, and skippable otherwise. Cursor's agent best-practices says not every task needs a detailed plan and quick or familiar changes can go straight to the agent. If the build goes wrong, revert, refine the plan and rerun instead of patching with follow-ups. VS Code docs say to plan when the approach is uncertain or the change spans multiple parts, and to implement directly for small, well-defined edits.
findings.evidence: Cursor page: Plan Mode toggled with Shift+Tab, plans saved to .cursor/plans/, 'Not every task needs a detailed plan'. VS Code page: Plan agent researches, asks clarifying questions, produces steps, files and verification steps for review before any implementation.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Industry norm is a user or heuristic trigger, not an always-on plan. Mirror that with a trigger set: ambiguity, multi-file scope, unfamiliar area, missing tests, risky domain (billing, auth, migrations). Cursor's 'revert and re-plan' is a cheap escalation path: fast path first, escalate to full flow if the check fails, instead of paying for the full flow up front.

findings.claim: Aider's architect/editor split is the one case with published numbers where a plan-then-execute split helped. On Aider's code-editing benchmark, o1-preview solo scored 79.7% and o1-preview as architect with an editor model scored 85.0%. Sonnet 3.5 self-paired went from 77.4% to 80.5%, GPT-4o from 71.4% to 75.2%. The stated reason was that reasoning models solve well but format edits badly, so a second model produces the edits. A later post (Jan 2025) says o1 paired with Sonnet did not beat o1 alone, and the split is optional (single model by default).
findings.evidence: Benchmark figures fetched from the Sept 2024 post; the Jan 2025 claim comes from the search snippet of the r1-sonnet post and was not fetched in full.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: The gain came from separating reasoning from edit formatting, not from review ceremony, and it shrank with stronger models. With modern Opus or Sonnet writing edits well, the Haiku-executor split saves money but needs verification to hold quality. Keep the split for hard tasks where the strong model's design matters, and drop it when one agent handles the whole task. Aider results are Aider's own benchmark on 2024 models.

findings.claim: OpenAI reports GPT-5-Codex adapts its thinking time by task: on the bottom 10% of turns by generated tokens it used 93.7% fewer tokens than GPT-5, and on the top 10% it spent about twice as long reasoning, editing, testing and iterating. Codex docs now say light/low effort suits quick, well-scoped tasks, medium balances speed and depth, high and extra high suit difficult multi-step work, and max or ultra are rarely needed. They also say effort levels do not map exactly across model generations and recommend testing a familiar task at a lower setting.
findings.evidence: 93.7% and 2x figures come from InfoQ's report of OpenAI's data (the openai.com announcement returned HTTP 403, so primary figures are second-hand). The effort guidance was read directly from the Codex models page.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Gives an upper bound on what difficulty-adaptive compute can save on easy work (token cost on the easiest tasks falls by an order of magnitude) and shows that the trade is symmetric: hard tasks get more compute, not less. Matches the goal that simple tasks skip ceremony while hard tasks keep the full flow. The 93.7% is for one model's internal reasoning, not for multi-agent ceremony, so do not use it as a projected saving.

findings.claim: Devin 2.0 uses an interactive planning step at session start (researches the codebase, returns relevant files, findings and a preliminary plan within seconds, editable by the user), then runs autonomously. Devin's instructing guide stresses specific, scoped, verifiable sub-tasks with success criteria and checkpoints, tests, lint, builds and CI as feedback loops, and having Devin verify its own work before opening a PR. Splitting large work into one session per sub-task reduces errors.
findings.evidence: Pages describe interactive planning and scoping advice; neither page states cost or latency numbers, and confidence-rating details were not on the fetched pages.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: Devin's plan is a cheap research-then-plan step, not a multi-review chain. Consider a lightweight plan that comes from scouting output, with review gated on risk. The doc's advice to decompose into verifiable sub-tasks supports keeping the DAG for large tasks but not for tasks that are already a single verifiable unit.

findings.claim: Anthropic and Cursor both flag that each added review layer needs its own justification. Claude Code's guide says a reviewer prompted to find gaps will always report some and that chasing all of them causes over-engineering, so reviewers should flag only correctness or stated-requirement gaps. Anthropic's thinking docs warn that steering for less thinking may lower quality on tasks that benefit from reasoning and should be measured before shipping.
findings.evidence: Direct statements on both pages (adversarial review section; Warning box under 'Verify steering on your workload').
findings.implicationForGraphEng: This is the main quality risk of a fast path. Skipping plan and design review can let wrong-problem or missed-requirement bugs through, and a critic with no severity filter can add noise. Mitigate with an escalation rule (fast-path check fails or critic finds a correctness gap, then rerun with the full flow) and measure with the hidden-test benchmarks, which were built for false DONE.

findings.claim: No source found quantifies, in production coding agents, the savings of skipping planning on simple tasks. Public figures are: Anthropic's effort-parameter token savings on SWE-bench (Opus 4.5), OpenAI's 93.7% fewer tokens on easy turns, Anthropic's 15x token cost of multi-agent vs chat, and Aider's benchmark gains from planning on 2024 models. The searches turned up no controlled study on plan-vs-no-plan failure rates for simple versus hard tasks.
findings.source: Absence of results across searches in this session; related primary sources above
findings.evidence: Searches on Claude Code, Aider, Codex, Copilot, Cursor and Devin returned qualitative guidance only. Third-party pages (claudelog, mindstudio, tenten) gave conflicting thinking-budget figures (1,024/4,000/31,999 tokens) and were not used as findings.
findings.implicationForGraphEng: graph-eng will have to produce its own evidence. Run a paired benchmark (fast path vs full flow, several tasks per tier, repeated runs since n=1 is noisy) with cost, wall time, calls and hidden-test pass rate, and include tasks where planning should matter (ambiguous spec, multi-file, cross-module invariants) to catch the quality downside. Record the router's tier decision so mis-routes can be counted.
